title: Gentlest Route Across a Height Map
statement:
A hiker crosses a grid heights from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, stepping up, down, left or right one cell at a time. The strain of a route is the largest absolute height difference between two consecutive cells on it. Not the total: just the single worst step.

Return the smallest possible strain of any route.

examples.why: Going down and then right, 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 5, never changes by more than 1. The short way along the top would climb 9 at once.
Via 8 the steps are 7 and 6, so the strain is 7. Via 9 the steps are 8 and 7, so the strain is 8.
Start and end are the same cell. No steps, no strain.

hints: Fix a limit L. Can you check whether some route uses only steps of size at most L?
That check is a plain BFS that ignores steps above L. And if L works, every bigger L works too, so you can binary search on L.
Or skip the search: run Dijkstra where a path's cost is the maximum step so far instead of the sum. Cells pop off the heap in order of their best strain.

explain.intuition:
This is a shortest-path problem with a different way of adding up a path: the cost of a route is its worst edge, not the sum of its edges. Dijkstra still works, because extending a path can never make its maximum smaller. So the first time the target leaves the heap, its strain is final.

There is also a yes/no view. "Is there a route whose steps are all at most L?" is a reachability question you can answer with BFS, and the answer only flips once as L grows. Binary search over L finds the smallest one that works. A third view: add edges from gentlest to steepest with union-find, and stop when start and end join.
steps: Set best[start] = 0 and every other cell to infinity. Push (0, start) onto a min-heap.
Pop the cell with the smallest strain d. Skip it if d is larger than its stored best. If it is the target, return d.
For each neighbour, compute nd = max(d, |height difference|).
If nd beats the neighbour's best, store it and push it.
The loop always reaches the target, since the grid is connected.
pitfalls: Summing the step sizes. The strain is the maximum single step, as the second example shows.
Plain DFS with only right and down moves. The gentlest route may wind back up or to the left.
Running BFS with a visited set and no heap. The first visit is the fewest steps, not the gentlest route.

solutions.title: Binary search on the strain with BFS
solutions.idea: Binary search the limit L between 0 and 1 000 000. For each L, BFS using only steps of size at most L and check whether the target is reached.

solutions.title: Dijkstra with max instead of sum
solutions.idea: A path's cost is its largest step. Extending a path never lowers that, so Dijkstra's greedy order still holds.

solutions.title: Union-find over sorted steps
solutions.idea: Sort all neighbour pairs by height difference and join them in that order. The step that first connects start and end is the answer.

followups: Return the route itself, not just its strain.
Instead of the worst step, minimise the total climbing (only upward steps count). Which algorithm do you need now?
